views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Maintain the retaliatory tariffs already announced on $60B of US goods (effective June 1) and signal readiness for talks at the upcoming G20. Do not escalate further — the US has threatened tariffs on all remaining Chinese imports (~$300B) and has just weaponized technology supply chains via the Huawei entity list. Provoking additional escalation risks an outcome far worse than the current state. Preserve negotiating leverage for a G20 meeting between Trump and Xi.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading of +0.5 reflects the fact that the dispute has entered a qualitatively new and more dangerous phase. US tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese exports at 25% (Lists 1-3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10), and the US has begun preparing tariffs on all remaining Chinese imports (~$300B). More critically, on May 15 Trump signed Executive Order 13873 and Commerce added Huawei plus 70 affiliates to the Entity List, cutting them off from US suppliers without government approval. This targets China's 5G ambitions and tech self-sufficiency goals — a core strategic vulnerability. Huawei's dependence on US semiconductor components and software (Android) makes this a serious choke point.

However, the threat is mitigated by several factors. China's Q1 2019 GDP grew 6.4%, beating forecasts and matching Q4 2018. Industrial production surged 8.5% in March (strongest since July 2014). The stimulus pipeline is active (8.2 trillion yuan in Q1 credit). The government has fiscal and monetary room to cushion the blow. China has also demonstrated it can match US tariff moves symmetrically — the $60B retaliation covers 5,000+ US products including agricultural goods that hit US farm-belt political constituencies.

The action_score of -0.15 reflects a stance just below neutral: we have already retaliated (the $60B tariffs on May 13), which is appropriate and necessary. But further escalation — such as dumping US Treasuries, singling out Boeing, or imposing export controls on rare earths — would risk triggering the $300B tariff tranche and deeper technology decoupling. The rational path is to hold current retaliatory posture, avoid new escalatory steps, and pursue a G20 meeting where a face-saving framework can be negotiated. China's leverage is real but not unlimited; spending it now on escalation rather than preserving it for negotiations would be suboptimal.
key_factors: US tariffs now cover ~$250B of Chinese exports at 25% (List 3 raised May 10)
Huawei + 70 affiliates added to Entity List on May 15 — threatens China's 5G and tech supply chain
US preparing tariffs on all remaining ~$300B of Chinese imports
China Q1 GDP 6.4% beat expectations; industrial production surged 8.5% in March
April data shows softening: retail sales 7.2% (slowest in 16 years), IP fell to 5.4%
China announced retaliatory tariffs on $60B US goods effective June 1
G20 summit in Japan offers next opportunity for Trump-Xi meeting
US stock markets fell sharply on China retaliation (Dow -617 points on May 13)
Both sides suffering — Kudlow admitted 'both sides will suffer' on Fox News

sources_cited.excerpt: Trump tweets that negotiations are going 'too slowly' and that China is attempting to 'renegotiate.' Orders List 3 raised from 10% to 25% on May 10 and directs preparation of tariffs on remaining Chinese imports (~$300B).
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.
China announces it will raise retaliatory tariff rates on its ~$60B US-goods list (higher rates phased in; many effective June 1).
Trump signs Executive Order 13873 (securing information/communications technology supply chains). Commerce moves to restrict Huawei.

Retail sales grew by 7.2 percent year-on-year in April, significantly lower than the 8.7 percent growth recorded in March. Industrial production expanded by 5.4 percent, far lower than the 8.5 percent growth recorded in March.

China's gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 6.4 per cent in the first quarter compared to a year earlier... beating analysts' expectations of 6.3 per cent growth. Industrial production expanded 8.5 per cent in March from a year earlier, the strongest growth since July 2014.

The U.S. Commerce Department said on Wednesday it is adding Huawei Technologies Co Ltd and 70 affiliates to its so-called 'Entity List' - a move that bans the telecom giant from buying parts and components from U.S. companies without U.S. government approval.
